# Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer scientist known for developing some of the country's first high-performance computers during the Cold War. Born into a family of intellectuals and alpinists, he suffered blindness and hand paralysis during World War II while serving in the Polish Home Army, but recovered to pursue engineering. His breakthrough achievement was the construction of **AKAT-1** in 1959, the world's first differential equations analyzer based on transistors, which simulated complex dynamic processes like heat transfer. Following this success, he created the **AAH** (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) to improve weather forecasting precision.
Karpiński's most significant contribution was the design of **KAR-65** in 1968, a compact, asynchronous computer capable of 100,000 operations per second, built using domestic Polish transistors. Later, he founded the Microcomputers' Construction Plant to develop the **K-202** , a highly innovative minicomputer that utilized Intel 4004 chips, floating-point representation, and memory segmentation. Although only 30 units were produced due to political opposition and the rise of the Riad project, the K-202 was technically superior to competitors like the DEC PDP-11. Karpiński also invented the perceptron in Poland (1964) and contributed to the development of the APL programming language. Despite facing censorship and professional setbacks, his work laid the foundation for modern computing in Poland and earned him international recognition, including the Officer's Cross of Polonia Restituta.
